title: Cyber Crimes — Overview under IT Act, 2000

content.overview: Cyber crimes under the Information Technology Act, 2000 include tampering with computer source documents (s. 65), computer-related offences such as dishonestly or fraudulently doing any act under s. 43 (s. 66), identity theft (s. 66C), cheating by personation using computer resource (s. 66D), violation of privacy (s. 66E), cyber terrorism (s. 66F), and publishing or transmitting obscene or sexually explicit material in electronic form (ss. 67, 67A, 67B). Section 66A was struck down; do not treat it as operative law. Civil liability under s. 43 is distinct from criminal liability.
content.glance: Ask: (1) Which IT Act offence section? (2) Mens rea where required (dishonestly/fraudulently)? (3) Civil s. 43 also available? (4) Concurrent BNS offence?
content.study:
Map facts to the specific section. s. 66A is not good law. Always separate civil compensation (s. 43) from criminal prosecution.

No new case invented. Shreya Singhal context for s. 66A is a verification item — not invented here as a full holding.

sections.heading: Core offences
sections.body: s. 65 (source code); s. 66 (computer-related offence linked to s. 43 acts done dishonestly/fraudulently); ss. 66B–66F (stolen computer resource, identity theft, personation, privacy, cyber terrorism).

sections.heading: Obscenity cluster
sections.body: ss. 67, 67A, 67B — publishing/transmitting obscene or sexually explicit material, including depicting children — as enacted.

sections.heading: s. 66A status
sections.body: s. 66A is not operative following constitutional invalidation; do not charge or advise under s. 66A.

sections.heading: Civil parallel
sections.body: s. 43 provides civil compensation for specified computer wrongs without necessarily requiring criminal mens rea.

sections.heading: Method
sections.body: Identify the computer resource act; match section; check mens rea; consider concurrent general criminal law.

examples.title: Identity theft
examples.body: Fraudulent use of another person's electronic signature or password → s. 66C analysis; possible concurrent cheating offences under general criminal law.

hypotheticals.question: Can offensive speech online still be prosecuted under s. 66A?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. s. 66A is not operative law after constitutional invalidation; other provisions or general criminal law may apply only if their own ingredients are met.

distinctions.title: Criminal IT Act offences vs s. 43 civil liability
distinctions.left: Prosecution with prescribed mens rea and punishment.
distinctions.right: Compensation for specified acts causing damage without the same criminal threshold.

misconceptions.trap: s. 66A is still available for online insults.
misconceptions.correction: s. 66A is struck down and must not be treated as current law.
